approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a national scheme to confiscate assets from people linked to crime who cannot explain how they got them.
It would let Commonwealth, state and territory agencies share information and powers to investigate and seize unexplained wealth across jurisdictions.
States must refer power to the Commonwealth or adopt its laws to join the scheme, and each state decides which of its offences are covered.
Extends Commonwealth unexplained wealth orders to territory offences and offences in participating states.
Allows state and territory agencies to use Commonwealth information-gathering powers for unexplained wealth investigations.
Creates new equitable sharing arrangements for recovered proceeds among law enforcement entities.
Amends the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 to let agencies use intercepted information in unexplained wealth cases.
Sets out a two-step referral process for states joining before the bill is enacted.
Provides a process for states joining after enactment by adopting the amended Proceeds of Crime Act.
Law enforcement agencies in the Commonwealth, states and territories, and people linked to criminal activity who hold unexplained wealth.

The majority voted in favour of the main idea of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read it for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means they can now discuss it in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1819a/19bd027): > *The purpose of the [Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6133) (the Bill) is to amend the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (the POC Act), the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 (the TIA Act) and the Proceeds of Crime Regulations 2002 to establish a national cooperative scheme on unexplained wealth (NCSUW).* > *The NCSUW will not replace existing unexplained wealth regimes operating at Commonwealth level and in the states and territories, but is intended to operate concurrently with them and enhance them by providing a more coordinated scheme with information sharing, access to information gathering powers and sharing arrangements for seized assets available to participating jurisdictions.*

The Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 was moved to create a national cooperative scheme targeting organised crime, estimated to cost at least $36 billion annually. It enables cross-jurisdictional asset confiscation, enhanced information sharing, and equitable asset distribution, with New South Wales already introducing referring legislation.

The Labor opposition supported the Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 as a first step toward a national unexplained wealth scheme, with only New South Wales having opted in. Labor argued the bill helps take profit out of crime by targeting organised crime kingpins, and criticised the Turnbull government for cutting $139 million from the Australian Federal Police over four years, leading to a loss of 567 personnel.
The Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 ensures that criminals cannot keep the proceeds of their crimes.

The speaker argued the Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 is essential to combat serious and organised crime by stripping criminal assets through a reverse onus of proof. They noted no cases were brought under the 2009 version, the cost of organised crime was $15 billion annually, and the bill sets a national standard to close jurisdictional loopholes.

The Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 establishes a national cooperative scheme to extend Commonwealth unexplained wealth powers to state offences, but only New South Wales and the Northern Territory have joined so far. The speaker also criticised the government for cutting $139 million from the Australian Federal Police over four years and reducing 567 personnel, undermining law enforcement capacity.

The speaker supported the Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018, noting that crime generates $2.8–$6.3 billion annually and that the bill expands powers to target unexplained wealth nationally. They announced the Queensland Labor government will not grant a casino licence for the Sunshine Coast, and criticised Queensland for not signing up to the national unexplained wealth scheme or the Trade Union Joint Police Taskforce.

The Unexplained Wealth Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 will create a national approach to target unexplained wealth, enabling participating jurisdictions to work together to deprive criminals of their wealth regardless of where they operate.
